description: We are a group of friends and software development students passionate about technology, learning, and exploring new ideas. We enjoy problem-solving, software development, and taking on creative challenges. We believe in teamwork, collaboration, and combining different perspectives to build meaningful and innovative solutions. We are excited to put our skills to the test and make the most of this NASA Space Apps Challenge!
summary:
Flame in Freefall is a free, open-source web application that makes NASA’s microgravity combustion research easier to explore and understand. Our research console brings together 26 investigations from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository.
Users can rank investigations by relevance to spacecraft and lunar-habitat research, compare studies side by side, and read clearly labeled, human-reviewed AI summaries. An interactive map plots 333 experimental tests from PSI-159 by oxygen concentration and pressure, showing their overlap with expected lunar-base atmospheric conditions and highlighting gaps in experimental coverage.
We address the challenge by turning scattered scientific records into an accessible tool with links to original sources. The application distinguishes missing evidence from evidence of safety: it does not predict fire risk or claim that microgravity tests reproduce lunar gravity.
By helping students, educators, and researchers understand both the findings and their limitations, Flame in Freefall supports learning and better-informed fire-safety research for future space habitats.
details:
Flame in Freefall is a free, open-source research console that helps students, educators, and researchers explore NASA’s microgravity combustion evidence. We bring together 26 investigations from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, connecting research discovery, comparison, and experimental visualization in one interface.

Our goal is not to replace scientific judgment, but to make the evidence and its limitations easier to understand.

What it does and how it works

The application combines three complementary tools:

- Explainable relevance ranking: Users explore investigations through four research profiles: crew cabin, lunar base or pressurized rover, fire detection, and fire suppression. Scores show their contributing factors and are explicitly identified as a team-designed heuristic, not a NASA assessment.

- Side-by-side comparison: Users compare up to three investigations by objectives, fuels, experimental conditions, hardware, and measurements. Missing information is identified rather than guessed.

- Experimental coverage map: An interactive visualization plots 333 tests from PSI-159 by oxygen concentration and pressure. Users can examine recorded outcomes, filter results, and compare experimental coverage with expected lunar-base atmospheric conditions.

Investigation pages provide source links, DOIs, and plain-language summaries. AI-generated summaries are labeled and reviewed by a person against the source material.

A preprocessing pipeline converts cached PSI records and experimental tables into structured JSON files. The browser uses these files to calculate rankings, comparisons, and visualizations. No AI service runs inside the application.

What makes our approach different

Our distinctive contribution is the connection between finding relevant research, comparing its context, and inspecting the underlying experimental coverage.

We do not simply summarize papers or display an attractive chart. Users can move from a research question to a relevant investigation, examine available test conditions, and return to the original source.

We also make uncertainty part of the experience. An empty region on the map means “not tested,” not “safe.” The mapped tests involve gaseous fuels, not spacecraft materials, and microgravity results are not presented as lunar gravity experiments. These boundaries make the tool more useful without overstating what the evidence supports.

Benefits and intended impact

NASA’s open research becomes more valuable when more people can navigate it. Our console reduces the effort required to discover relevant investigations, supports classroom exploration, and helps researchers identify questions that existing experiments do not answer.

The intended impact is better-informed learning and research around fire safety in future space habitats not-operational fire-risk prediction or safety certification.

Tools and development

We built the application with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Recharts, using Node.js scripts for data processing and Vitest for automated testing. OpenSpec supported specification-driven development, while GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages support building and publishing the application.

Claude Code assisted with development, tests, and documentation. Google Gemini generated draft summaries from PSI source text for human review. The application requires no specialized hardware or runtime AI API key.

Team values and design decisions

Our approach reflects scientific honesty, transparency, accessibility, collaboration, and responsible innovation.

These values translate into concrete choices: traceable sources, visible ranking logic, explicit missing data, human-reviewed AI content, open-source code, and verified dataset licenses. We prioritized a working, understandable tool over unsupported predictions or unnecessary complexity.

Our future vision

We envision an extensible, community-informed exploration platform for combustion research. Future development could incorporate additional openly licensed experimental tables, richer comparisons, educational walkthroughs, and multilingual explanations.

We would seek feedback from educators and combustion researchers to improve usability and validate interpretation. Expansion would preserve our central principle: make scientific evidence more accessible without making it appear more certain than it is.
